title: Open files: find the entry square
outcomes: Names the entry square before placing a rook on an open file
Checks whether a pawn or minor piece covers the entry square
Counts attackers and defenders before capturing a blocking pawn

steps.text:
An open file is a road, not a prize. A rook standing on it does nothing until it can **land** on a square in the enemy camp, best of all on the seventh rank, where pawns and the king are cramped.
Before you double rooks, ask: **which square will my rook land on, and can the enemy cover it?**

steps.caption: White to move. Follow the rook.

line.say: The rook lands on c7. No Black piece attacks that square.
Black makes room for his king.
The rook takes b7. White has won a pawn.

steps.text:
The plan works when three things hold.
**Your rook gets to the file first.**
**The entry square is not guarded by a pawn or a minor piece.**
**Something is waiting there:** undefended pawns, or a king with no room.
If the entry square is covered, landing there can cost you the rook.

steps.title: Same rook, one change
steps.prompt: Black's knight stands on e8 instead of h5. Does Rc7 still win a pawn? Predict first, then check.

steps.text:
Sometimes a pawn blocks the file. Count first: if it has fewer defenders than you have attackers, take it with your cheapest piece first.
If another pawn protects it, taking it may only lose material. Players then undermine it with a pawn lever or, rarely, give up material to open the file, but only when the landing square wins at once.

steps.title: Same pawn, one change
steps.prompt: Black's b-pawn stands on b7 instead of b6, so it protects c6. Does the knight capture still win a pawn? Predict first, then check.
Before you looked: what did you expect to be guarding the entry square in the last position? Was it a pawn, a minor piece, or nothing?
